list.listitem: Benign brain tumors can present as an incidental finding, or with a wide range of neurologic and endocrine symptoms related to the tumor histology, size, and location. C
Surgery is generally the primary treatment, but radiation therapy, medical therapy, and observation are appropriate and effective alternatives in some situations. C

background.definition: A slow-growing intracranial neoplasm lacks the ability to invade surrounding structures. The most common benign brain tumors are meningiomas, pituitary adenomas, and nerve sheath tumors.

list.listitem: Nonmalignant brain tumors occur at an incidence of 7.4 per 100,000 person years and account for half of all intracranial tumors.
Incidence of meningioma increases with age. Autopsy studies have found a 2% to 3% incidence of incidental asymptomatic meningiomas.
Incidence in United States is 97.5 per 100,000 persons.
Of benign brain tumors, 57% are meningiomas (2.8 times more common in women than men), 15% are nerve sheath tumors, and 12% are pituitary adenomas.
For most benign brain tumors, the etiology is unknown.
The only firmly established risk factors are the presence of a genetic predisposition and exposure to ionizing radiation. These causes are responsible for only a fraction of the total incidence.
Other suggested risks include chemical exposures, exposure to nonionizing radiation, trauma, and infectious causes.
The neoplastic transformation of benign brain tumors is thought to result from a multistep process of genetic alteration.
Meningiomas demonstrate a proliferative response with exposure to endogenous or exogenous sex hormones.
Benign brain tumors present with a wide variety of neurologic symptoms (eg, seizure or visual field loss) and/or endocrine symptoms related to the tumor histology and location. C
In most cases, the diagnosis is best established with a gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI. B
The clinical presentation of a benign brain tumor depends on the tumor location and histology.

Meningiomas present with a wide range of symptoms resulting from compression/irritation of the adjacent brain, or obstruction of the CSF pathways or vascular structures. Irritation of the underlying cortex can result in seizures. Compression of the underlying cortex can result in generalized symptoms such as weakness, somnolence, or cognitive changes. Obstructive hydrocephalus can result in a generalized headache, blurred vision, and nausea. Focal neurologic defecits can also result from local compression.

The majority of pituitary adenomas is secretory. The most common secretory product is prolactin, followed by growth hormone. Enlarging pituitary adenomas results in visual field deficits secondary to compression of the optic apparatus. Headaches are another common symptom. Older patients with pituitary adenoma (over age 65) are more likely to present with mass effects, and are less likely to have hormone secreting related symptoms.
Vestibular schwannomas commonly present with ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Tinnitus, dysequilibrium, and deficits of cranial nerves V and VII are also common complaints.
Benign brain tumors are typically diagnosed upon imaging with CT and/or gadolinium-enhanced MRI.

Meningiomas are dural based lesions that are hyperdense and uniformly enhancing on CT. Signal intensity is variable on T1 and T2 MRI sequences. Meningiomas enhance intensely and homogeneously with gadolinium.

If the history and physical exam suggests a secretory pituitary adenoma, serum hormone levels can be measured. If growth hormone hypersecretion is suspected, serum insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I) should be measured. Serum prolactin can be measured in the case, where lactotroph adenoma is suspected. If the laboratory evaluation is abnormal or if a space occupying lesion is suspected, then the patient should be evaluated with a gadolinium-enhanced MRI.
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the recommended diagnostic test for vestibular schwannomas. Thin cuts through the internal auditory canal should be included.
Many meningiomas are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally. Symptomatic meningiomas present most commonly with seizure or focal neurologic deficits.
Pituitary adenomas are often secretory and present with symptoms related to abnormal hormone levels. Enlarging pituitary tumors often present with visual field defects.
Vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) typically present with gradual onset of unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
MRI is the recommended initial imaging study for most patients.
Surgery is the initial treatment of choice for most benign brain tumors. A
Radiation therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery are useful alternatives. B
Medical management is often the first-line treatment for pituitary prolactinomas. C
Some benign brain tumors can be appropriately managed with observation only. B
Prolactinomas often shrink in response to medical therapy with dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine or cabergoline. Drug therapy is often the first-line treatment for prolactinomas.

Pharmacologic therapy for adenomas secreting growth hormone is used when surgery alone is not effective in reducing GH and IGF-1 to normal levels. The role of medical therapy in the primary treatment for growth hormone adenomas is not well established.

A meta-analysis of the use of pasireotide (a novel somatostatin receptor ligand) demonstrated effective responses in approximately 40% of patients with acromegaly or Cushing's disease. The proposal was that this medical therapy may be helpful in the situation of progressive growth, extrasellar extension or when the tumour is deemed unresectable or significant residual volume remains after surgery,

Symptomatic meningiomas and asymptomatic meningiomas that are expanding should be surgically resected if possible. Radiation therapy, stereotactic radiosurgery, observation, and chemotherapy are alternatives. Risk for recurrence after surgery is directly related to the completeness of the resection.

The primary treatment for pituitary adenoma is usually surgery. The transphenoidal approach is typically employed, and is endorsed by NICE guidelines. The most common complication is damage to the normal pituitary gland.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of surgery for prolactinomas included 12 studies and 1010 participants. Evaluating the biochemical remission rate post-surgery demonstrated higher remission rates in those patients with lower grade disease (Knosp grade 0-2 as compared to grades 3-4).

The recommended treatment for vestibular schwannoma is surgery. The major surgical morbidities are hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, facial weakness, and numbness. The risk for complications is related to tumor size.

A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating stereotactic radiosurgery in vestibular Schwannomas demonstrated 91% response in successful reduction in size or stabilisation, but was less effective if the tumor was fast growing.
In a nationwide database of pituitary tumour surgery including 14,947 individuals, it was demonstrated that institutional case load volume correlated with risk of operative complications.

Many meningiomas are asymptomatic and demonstrate indolent tumor growth. Asymptomatic meningiomas can be observed and only treated if growth is detected or if the lesion becomes symptomatic. Patients selected for observation should be reimaged 3 to 6 months later, and then annually if no growth is detected.

Radiation therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery have been commonly employed as an alternative to surgery, or as an adjuvant therapy for incompletely resected meningiomas. Control rates and complication rates comparable to surgery have been observed for small- and medium-sized tumors.

Vestibular schwannomas can be treated with radiation therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery as an alternative to surgery. Reported control rates are comparable, but long-term data are still accumulating.

A meta-analysis of 14 trials of resection of vestibular Schwannomas showed that 26% regrow and that the single predictive factor for recurrence was residual volume post-operatively. This led the authors to propose close follow-up with annual MR imaging.

A systematic review of gamma knife surgery for vestibular schwannoma found an overall hearing preservation rate of 51%, which was not associated with tumor volume or patient age. Lower doses of radiation (≤13 Gy) were associated with a greater likelihood of hearing preservation.
Patients with a new diagnosis of a symptomatic benign brain tumor should be referred for a neurosurgical evaluation.
An endocrinology referral is needed for patients with secretory pitutary adenomas.
Seizure prophylaxis is not recommended in patients with a newly diagnosed brain tumor.
If seizure medications are used perioperatively, they should be tapered and discontinued after the first postoperative week.
Some untreated benign brain tumors will show indolent growth patterns, but others will gradually enlarge resulting in neurologic deficits. B
Complete surgical resection and the alternative radiation treatments are usually curative. B
Untreated, asymptomatic benign meningiomas may or may not demonstrate growth with observation only. Growth occurs at a variable rate, ranging from 0 to 10 mm in diameter annually.
With observation only, 43% of vestibular schwannomas will demonstrate some growth. Of tumors that grow, the reported average growth rate is 1.9 mm per year.

Complete surgical resection for a benign meningioma nearly always results in permanent local control. Mortality associated with meningioma surgery ranges from 1% to 14% and depends largely on patient's age and preoperative clinical condition. The most common medical complications include pneumonia, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, and arrhythmias. Risk of neurologic complications is related to tumor location and size.

Biochemical cure rates after transphenoidal resection for pituitary adenoma range from 50% to 90%. Radiotherapy results in similar cure rates, but may require 18 to 24 months or more for hormone levels to decrease to the normal range. Hypopituatarism is the most common complication after pituitary surgery or radiation.

Vestibular schwannomas treated with surgery or radiosurgery are controlled 97% to 99% of the time. Risks of cranial nerve palsies vary widely and are related to the size of the tumor. Rates of hearing preservation after surgery or radiosurgery range from 30% to 80%. Headache is relatively common after treatment, especially if younger, experiencing comorbid anxiety or depression, or previous diagnosis of headache disorder.
